subproblems.title: Restriction theory of currents of locally finite mass (Simon 2.7–2.9)
subproblems.statement: Let U ⊆ ℝ^P be open and k ∈ ℕ. (R0) If X ∈ D_k(U) has a measure representation (μ,v) (IsMeasureRepresentation), then M_W(X) < ∞ for every W ⊂⊂ U. (R1) Any two restrictions (IsRestriction) of X ∈ D_k(U) to the same set A are equal. (R2) If M_W(X) < ∞ for every W ⊂⊂ U, then there is a measure μ with IsMassMeasure X μ such that X has a restriction to every Borel set A, and every restriction S of X to a set A satisfies M_W(S) = μ(W ∩ A) for every open W ⊆ U.
subproblems.lean_statement: (∀ (P k : ℕ) (U : Set (Eucl P)), IsOpen U → ∀ (X : GeometricCurrentOn U k) (μ : Measure (Eucl P)) (v : Eucl P → NVector (Eucl P) k), IsMeasureRepresentation X μ v → ∀ W, CompactlyContainedOpen W U → X.massOn W < ∞) ∧ (∀ (P k : ℕ) (U : Set (Eucl P)), IsOpen U → ∀ (X : GeometricCurrentOn U k) (A : Set (Eucl P)) (S₁ S₂ : GeometricCurrentOn U k), IsRestriction X A S₁ → IsRestriction X A S₂ → S₁ = S₂) ∧ (∀ (P k : ℕ) (U : Set (Eucl P)), IsOpen U → ∀ X : GeometricCurrentOn U k, (∀ W, CompactlyContainedOpen W U → X.massOn W < ∞) → ∃ μ : Measure (Eucl P), IsMassMeasure X μ ∧ (∀ A : Set (Eucl P), MeasurableSet A → ∃ S : GeometricCurrentOn U k, IsRestriction X A S) ∧ ∀ (A : Set (Eucl P)) (S : GeometricCurrentOn U k), IsRestriction X A S → ∀ W : Set (Eucl P), IsOpen W → W ⊆ U → S.massOn W = μ (W ∩ A))

Its Lean proof is already comparator-accepted (axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound), so this split re-proves nothing.

The numbered proof below replaces the copied prose proof that the previous decomposition audit rejected.
- Part (R1) now localizes explicitly, as that audit required. For each test form, a smooth compactly supported cutoff χ equal to 1 on its support makes every coefficient χ v_l^I globally integrable. That gives finite signed measures, whose equality is proved by smooth testing, uniform approximation and Riesz uniqueness. The restriction integrals are then recovered on the test-form support.
- Part (R0) uses the same cutoff.
- The "≥" half of the mass identity in (R2) follows the idea of the accepted Lean proof (X = S_A + S_{Aᶜ} plus an inner approximation) instead of Lusin's theorem.
Each part has a counterpart in the accepted Lean proof:
- R0: intOn, R0.
- R1: setInt, R1. These localize by restricting μ_l to closure W_i instead of using a cutoff.
- R2: extL, core, restrCur, massLe, massEq. massEq uses inner approximation by compact sets instead of the exhaustion of step 17.

Role in ind_md_mass_measure_balls (supplied step 2). Only (R2) is used, with P, k := n, U := univ (isOpen_univ) and X := T. Its hypothesis is supplied step 1: M_W(T) ≤ M(T) < ∞ by massOn_mono. It yields μ with IsMassMeasure T μ. The parent uses neither (R0), (R1) nor the restriction conclusions of (R2).

Conventions.
- ℝ^P := Eucl P, with standard orthonormal basis e_1,…,e_P.
- D^k(U) := TestFormOn U k: the smooth k-forms ω : ℝ^P → Λ^k(ℝ^P) with compact tsupport ω ⊆ U.
- D_k(U) := GeometricCurrentOn U k: the linear X : D^k(U) → ℝ with X(ω_j) → 0 whenever TestFormOnConverges ω_j 0. That convergence means all tsupport ω_j lie in one compact K ⊆ U and every iterated derivative of ω_j tends to 0 uniformly on K. Currents with equal values on all test forms are equal (GeometricCurrentOn.ext).
- I(k,P) is the set of strictly increasing maps {1,…,k} → {1,…,P}, and N := #I(k,P). For I ∈ I(k,P), e_I := (e_{I(1)},…,e_{I(k)}), and dx^I is the constant k-covector with dx^I(e_J) = δ_{IJ} (J ∈ I(k,P)). Every k-covector satisfies α = Σ_I α(e_I) dx^I (Submission.cmb_covector_eq_sum_coord_smul_wedge).
- |α| := covectorEuclideanNorm α = (Σ_I α(e_I)²)^{1/2}, so |α(e_I)| ≤ |α| (Submission.polyhedral_approx_pairing_coordinate_bound).
  - The coefficient map α ↦ (α(e_I))_I is a linear isometry of (Λ^k(ℝ^P), |·|) onto ℝ^N with the Euclidean norm. It is onto because Σ_I c_I dx^I has coefficient vector c.
  - For the operator norm ‖α‖, |α| ≤ √N′ ‖α‖, where N′ := #(Fin k → Fin P); this is because |α(e_I)| ≤ ‖α‖.
- For a form ω put ω_I(x) := ω(x)(e_I) and ‖ω‖_∞ := sup_x |ω(x)|. If ω is continuous with compact support, each ω_I is continuous, vanishes off tsupport ω and satisfies |ω_I| ≤ |ω|.
- A k-vector w ∈ NVector (Eucl P) k is a continuous linear functional on Λ^k(ℝ^P). Put w^I := w(dx^I); then w(α) = Σ_I α(e_I) w^I.
- IsMeasureRepresentation X μ v means: for every ω ∈ D^k(U), x ↦ v(x)(ω(x)) is μ-integrable and X(ω) = ∫ v(x)(ω(x)) dμ(x). Write v^I(x) := v(x)(dx^I); then v(x)(ω(x)) = Σ_I ω_I(x) v^I(x).
- ω ∈ D^k(U) is admissible for W if tsupport ω ⊆ W and |ω(x)| ≤ 1 for all x. M_W(X) := X.massOn W is the supremum of ofReal X(ω) over such ω, in [0, ∞]. M_W is monotone in W (massOn_mono), and ofReal X(ω) ≤ M_W(X) for admissible ω (le_massOn).
- W ⊂⊂ U := CompactlyContainedOpen W U: W is open, closure W is compact and closure W ⊆ U.
- IsRestriction X A S means: A is measurable, and some measure representation (μ, v) of X satisfies S(ω) = ∫_A v(x)(ω(x)) dμ(x) for all ω ∈ D^k(U).
- IsMassMeasure X μ means: μ(ℝ^P ∖ U) = 0 and μ(W) = M_W(X) for every W ⊂⊂ U.
- All measures are Borel measures on ℝ^P, except μ_0 (a measure on U) in steps 11–13.

Auxiliary facts. In (F1), (F3) and (F4), U ⊆ ℝ^P is open and X ∈ D_k(U).

(F1) Mass bound (Submission.cmb_abs_apply_le_of_massOn_le). Let V ⊆ ℝ^P with M_V(X) < ∞, and let ω ∈ D^k(U) with tsupport ω ⊆ V and |ω(x)| ≤ C for all x. Then |X(ω)| ≤ C·M_V(X).
Proof:
- C ≥ |ω(0)| ≥ 0.
- If C = 0, then ω = 0 because the coefficient map is injective, so X(ω) = 0.
- If C > 0, then ±ω/C are admissible for V, so ±X(ω)/C ≤ M_V(X).

(F2) Exhaustion. Let G ⊆ ℝ^P be open. There are open sets G_1 ⊆ G_2 ⊆ ⋯ with G_i ⊂⊂ G such that every compact K ⊆ G lies in some G_i; in particular ⋃_i G_i = G.
- Take G_i := {x : |x| < i and infEDist(x, ℝ^P ∖ G) > 1/(i+1)}; with ℝ^P ∖ G = ∅ the second condition always holds.
- These sets increase with i. Submission.cmb_exists_compactly_contained_exhaustion proves G_i ⊂⊂ G and the compact-covering property for exactly these sets. Monotonicity is not part of that lemma's statement, but it is clear from the formula, and it can also be forced by replacing G_i with G_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ G_i.
- If V, V′ ⊂⊂ G and W is open, then V ∪ V′ ⊂⊂ G and W ∩ V ⊂⊂ G, because a closed subset of a compact set is compact.
- We write W_1 ⊆ W_2 ⊆ ⋯ for the exhaustion of U itself.

(F3) Smooth cutoff. If K ⊆ U is compact, there is χ ∈ C^∞(ℝ^P) with 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ = 1 on K, and tsupport χ compact and contained in U.
Proof: take W_i ⊇ K from (F2) and apply exists_contDiff_support_eq_eq_one_iff to the open set W_i and the closed set K. This gives support χ = W_i, so tsupport χ = closure W_i, which is compact and contained in U.

(F4) Uniform approximation (Submission.cmb_exists_testForm_uniform_approx: a cutoff times a mollification). Let V ⊆ U be open, and let φ : ℝ^P → Λ^k(ℝ^P) be continuous with compact support and tsupport φ ⊆ V. For every ε > 0 there is ω ∈ D^k(U) with tsupport ω ⊆ V and |φ(x) − ω(x)| ≤ ε for all x. Likewise, standard mollification shows that every φ ∈ C_c(ℝ^P) is a uniform limit of functions in C_c^∞(ℝ^P).

Part (R0): a measure representation forces locally finite mass.

1. Integrable coefficients. Let (μ, v) be a measure representation of X ∈ D_k(U), and let W ⊂⊂ U.
   - Apply (F3) to K := closure W to obtain χ.
   - For each I ∈ I(k,P), the form χ dx^I is smooth and its tsupport lies in the compact set tsupport χ ⊆ U, so χ dx^I ∈ D^k(U).
   - Hence g^I(x) := v(x)(χ(x) dx^I) = χ(x) v^I(x) is μ-integrable.
   - Put C := Σ_I ∫ |g^I| dμ < ∞.

2. The bound. Let ω be admissible for W.
   - If x ∈ closure W, then χ(x) = 1, so v^I(x) = g^I(x).
   - If x ∉ closure W, then x ∉ tsupport ω, so every ω_I(x) = 0.
   - Hence v(x)(ω(x)) = Σ_I ω_I(x) g^I(x) for all x.
   - As |ω_I(x)| ≤ |ω(x)| ≤ 1, we get |v(x)(ω(x))| ≤ Σ_I |g^I(x)|.
   - So X(ω) = ∫ v(x)(ω(x)) dμ ≤ C. Taking the supremum gives M_W(X) ≤ ofReal C < ∞.

Part (R1): restrictions are unique (explicitly localized).

3. Setting. Let S_1 and S_2 be restrictions of X to the same set A.
   - So A is measurable, and for l = 1, 2 some measure representation (μ_l, v_l) of X satisfies S_l(ω) = ∫_A v_l(x)(ω(x)) dμ_l for all ω.
   - Fix ω ∈ D^k(U) and put K := tsupport ω, a compact subset of U.
   - By (F3) choose χ ∈ C^∞(ℝ^P) with 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ = 1 on K, and tsupport χ compact and contained in U.

4. Global integrability. For each I, the form χ dx^I lies in D^k(U), as in step 1.
   - So f_l^I(x) := v_l(x)(χ(x) dx^I) = χ(x) v_l^I(x) is μ_l-integrable on all of ℝ^P, for l = 1, 2.
   - Only these localized coefficients are integrated over all of ℝ^P; the coefficients v_l^I themselves need not be integrable there.
   - Being μ_l-integrable, f_l^I agrees μ_l-a.e. with a Borel function f̂_l^I. Integrals of f_l^I times a bounded Borel function do not change when f_l^I is replaced by f̂_l^I.

5. Finite signed measures. Put f̂_l^{I,±} := max(±f̂_l^I, 0), and for Borel B ⊆ ℝ^P put ν_l^{I,±}(B) := ∫_B f̂_l^{I,±} dμ_l.
   - These are finite positive Borel measures, since ν_l^{I,±}(ℝ^P) ≤ ∫ |f_l^I| dμ_l < ∞.
   - So ν_l^I := ν_l^{I,+} − ν_l^{I,−}, with ν_l^I(B) = ∫_B f_l^I dμ_l, is a finite signed Borel measure on ℝ^P.
   - For every bounded Borel h, ∫ h f_l^I dμ_l = ∫ h dν_l^{I,+} − ∫ h dν_l^{I,−}, and all three terms are finite.

6. Smooth testing. Let φ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^P).
   - The form φχ dx^I is smooth, and its tsupport lies in tsupport χ, which is compact and contained in U. So φχ dx^I ∈ D^k(U).
   - Its pairing with v_l is v_l(x)(φ(x)χ(x) dx^I) = φ(x) f_l^I(x).
   - Both representations compute X on this form, so ∫ φ f_1^I dμ_1 = X(φχ dx^I) = ∫ φ f_2^I dμ_2.

7. Uniform approximation. Let φ ∈ C_c(ℝ^P), and choose φ_j ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^P) with sup|φ_j − φ| → 0 (F4).
   - Then |∫ φ_j f_l^I dμ_l − ∫ φ f_l^I dμ_l| ≤ sup|φ_j − φ| · ∫ |f_l^I| dμ_l → 0.
   - With step 6, ∫ φ f_1^I dμ_1 = ∫ φ f_2^I dμ_2 for every φ ∈ C_c(ℝ^P).
   - This is the accepted Submission.slicing_ru_smooth_to_continuous with O := ℝ^P.

8. Riesz uniqueness. Let λ_1 := ν_1^{I,+} + ν_2^{I,−} and λ_2 := ν_2^{I,+} + ν_1^{I,−}; these are finite Borel measures on ℝ^P.
   - Rearranging finite terms in steps 5 and 7 gives ∫ φ dλ_1 = ∫ φ dλ_2 for every φ ∈ C_c(ℝ^P).
   - Agreement on open sets. Let O ⊆ ℝ^P be open, and put φ_j(x) := min(1, j·dist(x, ℝ^P ∖ O)) · max(0, min(1, j + 1 − |x|)). If O = ℝ^P, the first factor is 1.
     - Each φ_j is continuous, supported in the closed ball of radius j + 1, and satisfies 0 ≤ φ_j ≤ 1.
     - If x ∈ O, then φ_j(x) = 1 for all large j. If x ∉ O, then φ_j(x) = 0.
     - By dominated convergence (λ_l finite), λ_1(O) = lim ∫ φ_j dλ_1 = lim ∫ φ_j dλ_2 = λ_2(O).
   - The open sets form a π-system that contains ℝ^P and generates the Borel σ-algebra. So λ_1 = λ_2 by uniqueness of finite measures (MeasureTheory.ext_of_generate_finite). This is the uniqueness half of the Riesz representation theorem for finite Borel measures on ℝ^P.
   - Hence ∫ h dλ_1 = ∫ h dλ_2 for every bounded Borel h. By step 5, after rearranging finite terms, ∫ h f_1^I dμ_1 = ∫ h f_2^I dμ_2. That is, ν_1^I = ν_2^I tested against bounded Borel functions.
   - This is the accepted Submission.slicing_ru_continuous_to_bounded with O := ℝ^P, whose proof uses the same measures λ_1, λ_2.

9. Recovery on the test-form support.
   - If x ∈ K, then χ(x) = 1, so v_l^I(x) = f_l^I(x). If x ∉ K, then ω(x) = 0 and every ω_I(x) = 0.
   - Hence v_l(x)(ω(x)) = Σ_I ω_I(x) f_l^I(x) for every x.
   - Each h_I := 1_A ω_I is bounded and Borel, so each h_I f_l^I is μ_l-integrable, and
     S_l(ω) = ∫ 1_A(x) v_l(x)(ω(x)) dμ_l = Σ_I ∫ h_I f_l^I dμ_l.
   - By step 8 with h := h_I for each I, the right side is the same for l = 1 and l = 2. So S_1(ω) = S_2(ω).
   - Since ω ∈ D^k(U) was arbitrary, S_1 = S_2 (GeometricCurrentOn.ext).

Part (R2): mass measure, existence of restrictions, mass identity. Assume M_W(X) < ∞ for every W ⊂⊂ U. Let 𝒞 be the set of continuous φ : ℝ^P → Λ^k(ℝ^P) with compact support and tsupport φ ⊆ U. Write ‖φ‖_∞ := sup_x |φ(x)|.

10. Extension of X to 𝒞. Let φ ∈ 𝒞. Say that a sequence (ω_j) in D^k(U) approximates φ in V if V ⊂⊂ U, tsupport ω_j ⊆ V for all j, and ‖ω_j − φ‖_∞ → 0.
    - Approximations exist: choose W_i ⊇ tsupport φ by (F2), and apply (F4) with V := W_i and ε := 1/j.
    - Cauchy property. Let (ω_j) approximate φ in V. Since tsupport(ω_j − ω_m) ⊆ V, (F1) gives |X(ω_j) − X(ω_m)| = |X(ω_j − ω_m)| ≤ M_V(X)·‖ω_j − ω_m‖_∞. So (X(ω_j)) is Cauchy.
    - Independence. If (ω′_j) approximates φ in V′, then V ∪ V′ ⊂⊂ U and |X(ω_j) − X(ω′_j)| ≤ M_{V∪V′}(X)·‖ω_j − ω′_j‖_∞ → 0. So L(φ) := lim_j X(ω_j) does not depend on the approximation.
    - Linearity. If (ω_j) approximates φ in V and (η_j) approximates ψ in V′, then (aω_j + bη_j) approximates aφ + bψ in V ∪ V′. So L is linear.
    - L(ω) = X(ω) for every ω ∈ D^k(U): use the constant sequence and some W_i ⊇ tsupport ω.

    (10a) If V ⊂⊂ U, tsupport φ ⊆ V and |φ| ≤ c everywhere, then |L(φ)| ≤ c·M_V(X). Indeed, (F4) in V gives approximants with ‖ω_j − φ‖_∞ ≤ 1/j. Then |ω_j| ≤ c + 1/j, and (F1) applies.

    (10b) If O ⊆ U is open, tsupport φ ⊆ O and |φ| ≤ 1 everywhere, then ofReal L(φ) ≤ M_O(X).
    - This is trivial if M_O(X) = ∞.
    - Otherwise, apply (F2) to the open set O to get V ⊂⊂ O with tsupport φ ⊆ V; then V ⊂⊂ U.
    - Approximants ω_j from (F4) in V satisfy |ω_j| ≤ 1 + 1/j, so ω_j/(1 + 1/j) is admissible for O.
    - Hence ofReal X(ω_j) ≤ (1 + 1/j)·M_O(X). Letting j → ∞ gives ofReal L(φ) ≤ M_O(X).

11. Riesz representation on U. With the subspace topology, U is a locally compact, σ-compact Hausdorff space (it is open in ℝ^P).
    - Identification with 𝒞. For f ∈ C_c(U; ℝ^N), define f̃ : ℝ^P → Λ^k(ℝ^P) by f̃(x) := Σ_I f_I(x) dx^I for x ∈ U and f̃(x) := 0 otherwise.
      - f̃ ∈ 𝒞: it is continuous on the open set U and vanishes on the open set ℝ^P ∖ spt f, and these two open sets cover ℝ^P.
      - tsupport f̃ ⊆ spt f, a compact subset of U, and |f̃(x)| = |f(x)|.
      - Conversely, every φ ∈ 𝒞 equals f̃ for f := (φ(·)(e_I))_I restricted to U, with spt f = tsupport φ.
    - The functional. Λ(f) := L(f̃) is linear on C_c(U; ℝ^N).
      - Let K ⊆ U be compact, and choose W_i ⊇ K by (F2). By (10a), Λ(f) ≤ M_{W_i}(X) < ∞ whenever |f| ≤ 1 and spt f ⊆ K.
      - So Λ satisfies the hypothesis of the Riesz Representation Theorem (Simon Ch. 1, 4.14; SimonGMT simon_theorem_4_14). There, the locally compact Hausdorff space is U (not to be confused with the current X) and the Hilbert space is H := ℝ^N.
    - What the Riesz theorem gives. Its proof provides a Radon measure μ_0 on the Borel sets of U: SimonGMT vectorFunctionalEnvelopeMeasure, a regular measure, so it is inner regular on open sets by compact sets. It satisfies
      (∗) sup{Λ(f) : f ∈ C_c(U; ℝ^N), |f| ≤ g} = ∫_U g dμ_0 for every continuous compactly supported g : U → [0, ∞).
      This is the display (∗) in Simon's proof of 4.14 (SimonGMT simon_theorem_4_14_positive_envelope).
      For the same μ_0, the proof also provides a vector field ν : U → ℝ^N (SimonGMT simon_theorem_4_14_bounded_caratheodory):
      - ν is measurable for the σ-algebra of μ_0-measurable (Carathéodory) sets;
      - |ν| ≤ 1 everywhere;
      - Λ(f) = ∫_U ⟨f, ν⟩ dμ̄_0 for every f ∈ C_c(U; ℝ^N), where μ̄_0 is the Carathéodory extension of μ_0.
      Simon's statement even gives |ν| = 1 μ_0-a.e., which is not needed.
    - Borel version. μ_0 is finite on compact sets and U is σ-compact, so μ_0 is σ-finite. μ_0 is also Borel regular. Hence every μ_0-measurable set differs from a Borel set by a subset of a Borel μ_0-null set, and ν agrees μ̄_0-a.e. with a Borel function.
      - Replace ν by such a Borel function, and set it to 0 where its norm exceeds 1. Then ν is Borel and |ν| ≤ 1 everywhere, and Λ(f) = ∫_U ⟨f, ν⟩ dμ̄_0 still holds.
      - For this Borel integrand, the integral against μ̄_0 equals the integral against μ_0, since the two measures agree on Borel sets.
      - So Λ(f) = ∫_U ⟨f, ν⟩ dμ_0 for every f ∈ C_c(U; ℝ^N), with ν Borel and |ν| ≤ 1.

12. μ_0 is the mass. Let O ⊆ U be open, and put s(O) := sup{Λ(f) : f ∈ C_c(U; ℝ^N), |f| ≤ 1, spt f ⊆ O} ∈ [0, ∞]. Taking f = 0 shows s(O) ≥ 0.
    - μ_0(O) ≥ s(O). Given such an f, Urysohn's lemma in U gives g ∈ C_c(U; [0,1]) with g = 1 on spt f and spt g ⊆ O. Then |f| ≤ g, so by (∗), Λ(f) ≤ ∫ g dμ_0 ≤ μ_0(O).
    - μ_0(O) ≤ s(O). For a compact K ⊆ O, take such a g with g = 1 on K. Every f with |f| ≤ g has spt f ⊆ spt g ⊆ O and |f| ≤ 1. So μ_0(K) ≤ ∫ g dμ_0 = sup{Λ(f) : |f| ≤ g} ≤ s(O). Inner regularity of μ_0 on the open set O gives μ_0(O) ≤ s(O).
    - s(O) = M_O(X).
      - "≤" is (10b), since f̃ ∈ 𝒞, tsupport f̃ ⊆ O and |f̃| ≤ 1.
      - "≥": every ω admissible for O equals f̃ for some f with |f| ≤ 1 and spt f ⊆ O, and then Λ(f) = L(ω) = X(ω).
    - Hence μ_0(O) = M_O(X) for every open O ⊆ U.

13. The mass measure. Define the Borel measure μ on ℝ^P by μ(B) := μ_0(B ∩ U). This is the push-forward of μ_0 under the inclusion U ⊆ ℝ^P; U is open, hence Borel.
    - μ(ℝ^P ∖ U) = 0.
    - By step 12, μ(W) = μ_0(W) = M_W(X) for every W ⊂⊂ U. So IsMassMeasure X μ holds.
    - μ(K) < ∞ for every compact K ⊆ U: K ⊆ W_i for some i, and μ(W_i) = M_{W_i}(X) < ∞.

14. Representation. Define v : ℝ^P → NVector (Eucl P) k by v(x)(α) := Σ_I α(e_I) ν_I(x) for x ∈ U, and v(x) := 0 for x ∉ U.
    - Each x ↦ v(x)(α) is Borel, and by Cauchy–Schwarz |v(x)(α)| ≤ |α|·|ν(x)| ≤ |α|.
    - Let ω ∈ D^k(U). The function x ↦ v(x)(ω(x)) = 1_U(x) Σ_I ω_I(x) ν_I(x) is Borel and bounded by ‖ω‖_∞ 1_{tsupport ω}. By step 13 it is μ-integrable.
    - Let f := (ω_I)_I restricted to U, so f̃ = ω. Then X(ω) = L(ω) = Λ(f) = ∫_U ⟨f, ν⟩ dμ_0 = ∫ v(x)(ω(x)) dμ(x).
    - Thus (μ, v) is a measure representation of X.

15. Existence of restrictions. For measurable A ⊆ ℝ^P put S_A(ω) := ∫_A v(x)(ω(x)) dμ.
    - S_A is linear on D^k(U), because the integrands are integrable by step 14.
    - Continuity. Suppose TestFormOnConverges ω_j 0, with compact K ⊆ U.
      - The zeroth derivatives converge uniformly on K, so sup_{x∈K} ‖ω_j(x)‖ → 0, and every ω_j vanishes off K.
      - Hence ‖ω_j‖_∞ ≤ √N′ · sup_{x∈K} ‖ω_j(x)‖ → 0, and |S_A(ω_j)| ≤ ‖ω_j‖_∞ · μ(K) → 0.
    - So S_A ∈ D_k(U), and IsRestriction X A S_A holds via (μ, v).

16. Upper bound. Let A and W be measurable. Then M_W(S_A) ≤ μ(W ∩ A).
    - Let ω be admissible for W. Since ω vanishes off tsupport ω ⊆ W, |v(x)(ω(x))| ≤ |ω(x)| ≤ 1_W(x).
    - Hence ofReal S_A(ω) ≤ ∫_A 1_W dμ = μ(W ∩ A).

17. Lower bound. Let A be measurable.
    - First let V ⊂⊂ U. For every ω, X(ω) = ∫ v(ω) dμ = S_A(ω) + S_{Aᶜ}(ω), so ofReal X(ω) ≤ ofReal S_A(ω) + ofReal S_{Aᶜ}(ω).
    - Taking the supremum over ω admissible for V, and applying step 16 to Aᶜ:
      M_V(X) ≤ M_V(S_A) + M_V(S_{Aᶜ}) ≤ M_V(S_A) + μ(V ∖ A).
    - We have μ(V ∩ A) + μ(V ∖ A) = μ(V) = M_V(X), and μ(V ∖ A) ≤ μ(closure V) < ∞. Subtracting the finite term μ(V ∖ A) gives μ(V ∩ A) ≤ M_V(S_A).
    - Now let W ⊆ U be open. The sets V_i := W ∩ W_i (from (F2)) satisfy V_i ⊂⊂ U, increase with i, and have union W ∩ U = W.
    - By continuity from below and monotonicity of massOn,
      μ(W ∩ A) = sup_i μ(V_i ∩ A) ≤ sup_i M_{V_i}(S_A) ≤ M_W(S_A).
    - Together with step 16, M_W(S_A) = μ(W ∩ A).

18. Any restriction. Let S be any restriction of X to a set A; then A is measurable. S_A is also a restriction of X to A (step 15), so S = S_A by (R1). Hence M_W(S) = μ(W ∩ A) for every open W ⊆ U.

19. Conclusion. Steps 13, 15 and 18 give (R2). Together with (R0) and (R1), this proves all three conjuncts. ∎
proof_key_steps: (R0) A cutoff χ with χ = 1 on closure W makes each χv^I μ-integrable. Every admissible X(ω) is at most Σ_I ‖χv^I‖_{L¹(μ)}, so M_W(X) < ∞.

(R1) Localization: for a test form ω choose χ ∈ C^∞ with χ = 1 on tsupport ω and tsupport χ compact ⊆ U. Then χ dx^I ∈ D^k(U), so f_l^I := χv_l^I ∈ L¹(μ_l), and the coefficient signed measures ν_l^I := f_l^I μ_l are finite.

(R1) Testing X on φχ dx^I gives ∫φ dν_1^I = ∫φ dν_2^I for φ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^P). Uniform approximation extends this to C_c. Riesz uniqueness (the finite measures ν_1^{I,+} + ν_2^{I,−} and ν_2^{I,+} + ν_1^{I,−} agree on open sets, then everywhere by π–λ) extends it to all bounded Borel h.
(R1) Recovery: on tsupport ω, v_l(ω) = Σ_I ω_I f_l^I. So S_l(ω) = Σ_I ∫ 1_A ω_I f_l^I dμ_l is the same for l = 1, 2, and S_1 = S_2 by GeometricCurrentOn.ext.

(R2) Using the mass bound (F1) and uniform approximation, X extends to a linear L on continuous compactly supported forms. Simon's Riesz theorem 4.14 on U gives a Radon μ_0 and a Borel ν with |ν| ≤ 1. The envelope identity (∗) and inner regularity give μ_0(O) = M_O(X) for every open O ⊆ U.
(R2) μ := μ_0(· ∩ U) satisfies IsMassMeasure X μ. With v(x)(α) := Σ_I α(e_I)ν_I(x), (μ, v) represents X, and S_A(ω) := ∫_A v(ω) dμ is a current and a restriction of X to A.
(R2) M_W(S_A) ≤ μ(W ∩ A) since |v(x)(α)| ≤ |α|. For V ⊂⊂ U, X = S_A + S_{Aᶜ} gives μ(V ∩ A) ≤ M_V(S_A); exhausting W by W ∩ W_i gives equality. Any restriction S of X to A equals S_A by (R1).

subproblems.title: A mass measure of a current on ℝ^P equals local mass on open balls and has total mass at most M(T)
subproblems.statement:
Let P, n ∈ ℕ, let T ∈ D_n(ℝ^P) (T : GeometricCurrentOn univ n on ℝ^P = Eucl P), and let μ be a measure on ℝ^P that is a mass measure of T (IsMassMeasure T μ with U = ℝ^P). That is: μ(ℝ^P ∖ ℝ^P) = 0, and μ(W) = M_W(T) (= T.massOn W) for every W ⊂⊂ ℝ^P (CompactlyContainedOpen W univ: W open, closure W compact, closure W ⊆ ℝ^P). Then:
- μ(ℝ^P) ≤ M(T) (= T.mass = T.massOn univ);
- μ(B_r(x)) = M_{B_r(x)}(T) (= T.massOn (ball x r)) for every x ∈ ℝ^P and every r ∈ ℝ, where B_r(x) is the open ball (empty when r ≤ 0).
No finiteness of M(T) is assumed.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (T : GeometricCurrentOn (univ : Set (Eucl P)) n) (μ : Measure (Eucl P)), IsMassMeasure T μ → μ univ ≤ T.mass ∧ ∀ (x : Eucl P) (r : ℝ), μ (ball x r) = T.massOn (ball x r)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 1, 3 and 4 of the supplied proof of ind_md_mass_measure_balls (itself Step 1, (1a)–(1b), of the proof of ind_mass_density_bound), applied to an arbitrary given mass measure μ. Cf. Simon Ch. 6, 2.8: μ_T(W) = M_W(T) for W ⊂⊂ U, and in particular μ_T(U) = M(T).

Conventions.
- ℝ^P := Eucl P = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin P).
- M_W(T) := T.massOn W for W ⊆ ℝ^P. This is the supremum in [0, ∞] of ofReal(T(ω)) over test forms ω with tsupport ω ⊆ W and covectorEuclideanNorm(ω(x)) ≤ 1 for all x (GeometricCurrentOn.massOn).
- M(T) := T.mass, which by definition (GeometricCurrentOn.mass) is M_{ℝ^P}(T) = T.massOn univ.
- 'W ⊂⊂ ℝ^P' means CompactlyContainedOpen W univ: W is open, closure W is compact, and closure W ⊆ univ.
- IsMassMeasure T μ (contract definition, U = univ) means μ(univᶜ) = 0 and μ(W) = M_W(T) for every W ⊂⊂ ℝ^P.
- B_r(x) := ball x r.

1. Monotonicity of local mass. Let W ⊆ ℝ^P. Since W ⊆ univ, every form admissible for M_W(T) is admissible for M_univ(T). So GeometricCurrentOn.massOn_mono gives M_W(T) ≤ M_univ(T) = M(T).

2. Open balls are compactly contained in ℝ^P. Fix x ∈ ℝ^P and r ∈ ℝ.
 (a) ball x r is open (isOpen_ball).
 (b) closure(ball x r) ⊆ closedBall x r (closure_ball_subset_closedBall: closedBall x r is closed and contains ball x r).
 (c) ℝ^P is a finite-dimensional real normed space, hence a proper metric space, so closedBall x r is compact (isCompact_closedBall).
 (d) closure(ball x r) is closed (isClosed_closure) and, by (b), contained in the compact set closedBall x r. So it is compact (IsCompact.of_isClosed_subset).
 (e) closure(ball x r) ⊆ univ trivially.
 Hence CompactlyContainedOpen (ball x r) univ. This also holds when r ≤ 0: then ball x r = ∅ and the same argument applies verbatim.

3. Ball values. By step 2 and the second component of IsMassMeasure T μ, μ(ball x r) = T.massOn (ball x r) for all x ∈ ℝ^P and r ∈ ℝ. This is the second conclusion.

4. Exhaustion by balls. For k ∈ ℕ put B_k := ball 0 (k : ℝ).
 - If k ≤ k′ then (k : ℝ) ≤ (k′ : ℝ) (Nat.cast_le), so B_k ⊆ B_{k′} (ball_subset_ball). Thus k ↦ B_k is monotone.
 - ⋃_k B_k = ℝ^P (iUnion_ball_nat): for y ∈ ℝ^P, the Archimedean property gives a natural k > dist y 0, and then y ∈ B_k.

5. Continuity from below. For a monotone sequence of sets indexed by ℕ, μ(⋃_k B_k) = sup_k μ(B_k) (Monotone.measure_iUnion). With step 4, μ(ℝ^P) = μ(⋃_k B_k) = sup_k μ(B_k).
 Lean remark: rewrite only the measured set, for example with calc μ univ = μ (⋃ k : ℕ, ball (0 : Eucl P) k) := by rw [iUnion_ball_nat]. A global rewrite of univ also hits the current's domain inside T.mass and fails with a motive error.

6. Total-mass bound. For each k, step 3 (with x = 0, r = k) and step 1 (with W = B_k) give μ(B_k) = M_{B_k}(T) ≤ M(T). Hence sup_k μ(B_k) ≤ M(T) (iSup_le), and by step 5 μ(ℝ^P) ≤ M(T). This is the first conclusion.

7. Steps 3 and 6 are the two conclusions. Neither the first component of IsMassMeasure (μ(univᶜ) = 0) nor any finiteness of M(T) is used. ∎
proof_key_steps: For every W ⊆ ℝ^P, M_W(T) ≤ M(T) (massOn_mono, since W ⊆ univ).
Every open ball ball x r (any r ∈ ℝ) is CompactlyContainedOpen in univ: it is open, and its closure is a closed subset of the compact closed ball closedBall x r (ℝ^P is proper).
The second component of IsMassMeasure T μ gives μ(ball x r) = T.massOn (ball x r).
The balls ball 0 k (k ∈ ℕ) increase and exhaust ℝ^P (ball_subset_ball, iUnion_ball_nat), so μ(ℝ^P) = sup_k μ(ball 0 k) (Monotone.measure_iUnion).
Each μ(ball 0 k) = M_{ball 0 k}(T) ≤ M(T), hence μ(ℝ^P) ≤ M(T).
